Having prostrated before the one-tusked God and likewise before my preceptor Śāradā, I compose this *Muhūrtadīpaka*, which dispels the darkness of ignorance for the young. *Śrīgaṇeśāya namaḥ*. The author of the work says: "I compose the *Muhūrtadīpaka*."

It is called *Muhūrtadīpaka* because it illuminates the auspicious moments (*muhūrta*) for the performance of sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) such as the birth ceremony (*jātakarma*). Having prostrated before the one-tusked god Gaṇeśa, the supreme Śāradā (Sarasvatī), and the Guru, [the author composes this work]. It is characterized as "removing the darkness of the ignorance of children" (*bālājñānatamopaha*), for it dispels that very darkness which is their ignorance. [Now follow] the things to be avoided on the lunar days beginning with Nandā.

The lunar days beginning with the first (pratipad) are known as Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, and Riktā, while the others are Pūrṇā; they accomplish purposes corresponding to their names when occurring on the days of Venus, Mercury, Earth-born (Mars), Sun, and Jupiter. Service to women, shaving, oil-massage, and battle are inauspicious on the New Moon, the fourteenth, the sixth, and the eighth days. Bathing is forbidden on the days of destruction (the fourteenth), the eyes (two), and the Creator (one), as well as on the limited lunar days numbering thirty, eight, and seven. *Muhūrtadīpaka*: The lunar days beginning with the first are called Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, and so forth, and the others are Riktā and Pūrṇā.

Those [tithis] which are oriented toward the path (pratipad) are as follows: here, the plural number is used because there are three called *nandā*, three called *bhadrā*, three called *jayā*, three *riktikās*, and three *pūrṇās*; these have functions corresponding to their names—that is, the accomplishment of tasks (*arthakṛtya*) in them corresponds to their respective names. These very tithis, beginning with *nandā*, become "accomplished" (*siddhāḥ*) if they fall on the days of Venus, Mercury, Mars, Saturn, Sunday, and Thursday respectively. *Nandā* [is auspicious] on Friday and Wednesday; *Bhadrā* on Tuesday; and *Jayā* on Saturday.

The lunar days (tithis) are empty on the day of the Guru (Jupiter) and full on the day of the Sun; thus the tithis are established in their respective order. On the new moon, the fourth, the sixth, and the eighth days, respectively, sexual intercourse with women, shaving, oil, and meat are declared inauspicious. As it has been said: "Sages declare that for men, using oil on the sixth days, performing the act of shaving on the eighth days, and indulging in women on the fourteenth days—when the digits [of the moon] have perished—leads to the destruction of one's lifespan."

"Āśā" refers to ten (10), "akṣi" to two (2), and "viśve" to thirteen (13). On the lunar days (tithis) delimited by these—namely the tenth, second, and thirteenth—one should not perform the *āmalaka* bath on those days that correspond to thirty (30), nine (9), or seven (7). As it has been said: "The tenth [lunar day] destroys the family of one who bathes, the thirteenth destroys wealth; likewise, the second destroys both."

"A person desiring prosperity should never, at any time, bathe with *āmalaka* fruits on the seventh, ninth, or fourteenth lunar days. (2) "In auspicious rites, the 'burnt' (*dagdha*) lunar days must be avoided. The 'burnt' days are the pairs [of tithis] when the Sun has entered Sagittarius, Pisces, Aquarius, Taurus, Gemini, Virgo, Libra, Capricorn, Aries, and Leo, respectively. The *Nandā* and other [classes of tithis], ending with the *Riktā*, are associated with the three [groups of] asterisms starting from Āśleṣā. (With commentary)

The first lunar days (pratipad) of the four [lunar months] are full and auspicious for me; however, the tooth-stick [should not be used] on the first day of a cruel zodiac sign, nor on the sixth day. Regarding the term "burnt" (*dagdhā*): the even lunar days—namely the second, fourth, sixth, eighth, tenth, and twelfth—are "burnt," provided that the sun has entered the pair of signs to be described hereafter. For example, when the sun is in Sagittarius and Pisces, the second day is "burnt"; "Sagittarius and Pisces" is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*).

When the Sun is in Aquarius (Ghaṭa) or Aries (Kumbha), the fourth lunar day is "burnt" (inauspicious); here, the term is a *itaretara-dvandva* compound. When the Sun is in Cancer (Kāñja) or Aries (Meṣa), the sixth lunar day is burnt. When the Sun is in Virgo (Strī) or Gemini (Nṛyugma), the eighth lunar day is burnt. When the Sun is in Leo (Mṛgapati) or Scorpio (Saviṣa), the tenth lunar day is burnt. When the Sun is in Libra (Tauli) or Capricorn (Nakra), the twelfth lunar day is burnt and forbidden. As it has been said: "In Pisces (Mīna) and Sagittarius (Cāpa), the second lunar day [is burnt]; and in Taurus (Vṛṣa) and Aquarius (Kumbha), the fourth."

The sixth lunar day (tithi) in Aries and Cancer, the eighth in Virgo and Gemini, the tenth in Scorpio and Leo, and the twelfth in Aquarius and Libra—these are the "burnt" (dagdha) tithis when the Sun is situated in each respective pair of signs. Furthermore, the four tithis beginning with Nandā and ending with Riktā occur three times in rotation starting from the sign of Aja (Aries): for the first four signs, Nandā belongs to Aries, Bhadrā to Taurus, Jayā to Gemini, and Riktā to Cancer; for the next four signs, Pūrṇā lasts for two praharas (six hours) in each case.

For the five signs beginning with Aries, [the lunar days] are up to the fifth. Likewise, for the four signs beginning with Leo, they are from the sixth onwards, and similarly, for the four signs beginning with Leo again, they are up to the tenth; and for the four signs beginning with Sagittarius, they are from the eleventh onwards. Furthermore, the full moon (Pūrṇā) occurs for the signs beginning with Sagittarius. Thus, one sign corresponds to one lunar day plus a quarter; this is known as the "sign with excess" (*rāśyādhika-saṃjñā*) in relation to a malefic sign—that lunar day associated with a sign that is joined by a malefic planet, namely Mars, Saturn, Rāhu, or Ketu.

One should not eat *camaka* on the first lunar day (*pratipad*), nor should one perform the brushing of teeth on the sixth or the tenth lunar days. Thus it is said in the *Muhūrtadīpaka*: "On the eighth, the sixth, the first lunar days, and the new moon, a wise person should never perform the scraping of teeth; by doing so, he surely incurs the destruction of his fortune, lineage, birth, and victory. (2) [Now follow] the lords of the constellations (*nakṣatra-svāmin*).

The lords of the asterisms (nakṣatras) are as follows: Aja, Dantaka, Aniduhina, Śaśin, Śiva, Deva, Sūri, Ījya, Sarpa, and the one called Pitṛ; then Bhaga, Aryaman, Ṛṣi, Diviṣat, Sraṣṭṛ, Kāra, Anila; Śakra, Agni, Mitra, Indra, Nirṛti, Tama, Udbhava, Vāri, Viśve, Vidhātṛ, Śrīśa, Vasu, Asya, Adāpati, Aja, Padahibudhnya, and Pūṣan. (Verse 4) Regarding the phrase "lords of the asterisms" (*bheśā*): these are to be known as the lords (*īśā*) of the measures, that is, the asterisms (*nakṣatras*).

Who are those ten? The Aśvinī-kumāras are the lords of Aśvinī; Antaka (Yama) is [the lord] of Bharaṇī; Agni is [the lord] of Kṛttikā; Druhiṇa (Brahmā) is [the lord] of Rohiṇī; Śaśin (the Moon) is [the lord] of Mṛgaśīrṣa; Śiva is [the lord] of Ārdrā—here there is a mutual dvandva compound. Devasū (Aditi), who gives birth to the gods, is [the lord] of Punarvasu; Ījya (Guru/Jupiter) is [the lord] of Puṣya; Sarpas are [the lords] of Āśleṣā; those called Pitṛs (the Ancestors) are [the lords] of Maghā; Maga, a specific form of the Sun, is [the lord] of Pūrvā-phālgunī; and Aryaman is [the lord] of Uttarā-phālgunī.

The Sun is the lord of Hasta; Viśvakarman, the architect of the gods (*diviṣad*), is the lord of Citrā; Vāyu (Anila) is the lord of Svāti; both Śakra and Viśvakarman are the lords of Viśākhā; Sūryamitra is the lord of Anurādhā; Manu is the lord of Jyeṣṭhā; the Rākṣasas, who dwell in the netherworld, are the lords of Mūla; Water (Vāri) is the lord of Pūrvāṣāḍhā; the Viśvedevas are the lords of Uttarāṣāḍhā; Vidhātṛ is the lord of Abhijit; Śrīśa (Viṣṇu) is the lord of Śravaṇa; [and] Svāsyā...

The Vasus are the presiding deities of Dhaniṣṭhā; Varuṇa, the lord of waters, is the deity of Śatatārakā (Śatabhiṣaj); Aja-Ekapāt, a form of Mahādeva, is the lord of Bhaga, the deity of Pūrvā-Bhādrapadā; Ahirbudhnya is the deity of Uttarā-Bhādrapadā; and Pūṣan, a form of Sūrya, is the deity of Revatī. Thus, the names of these twenty-eight deities should be assigned as the names of the [corresponding] lunar mansions. [Section 4: An investigation into the technical designations such as *parā* and others.

Svāti, Āditya (Punarvasu), and the triad of Haris (Śravaṇa) are *cara* (mobile); Dhātṛ (Rohiṇī) and the three Uttarās are *sthira* (fixed); Mṛgaśiras, Pūrvaphalgunī, and Antaka (Bharaṇī) are *miśraka* (mixed). Hasta, Jyeṣṭhā, Aśvinī, and Abhijit are *laghu* (light); Mṛgaśiras, Citrā, Anurādhā, and Maitra (Anurādhā) are *mṛdu* (soft); Jyeṣṭhā, Ārdrā, Āśleṣā, and Mūla—these are declared to be *tīkṣṇa* (sharp) according to Śaśin (the Moon). *Svāti*; *Āditya* means "belonging to Aditi," which is Punarvasu; by the word *hari*, the triad of Haris is to be understood as Śravaṇa.

This is a conventional treatise [whereby] the name of a whole is used to denote a single part. The triad of Śravaṇa—namely Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Śatabhiṣaj—these five lunar mansions are designated as "moving" (cara) and "unstable" (cala). Dhātṛ (Rohiṇī), the three Uttaras, and Ārdrā—these are designated as "fixed" (dhruva) and "stable" (sthira). Pitṛ (Maghā), the three Pūrvas, and Antaka (Bharaṇī)—this pentad is designated as "cruel" (krūra) and "fierce" (ugra).

Now, Dvīsha (Jyeṣṭhā), Viśākhā, and Anala (Kṛttikā)—these are known as the mixed group; Hasta, Ījya (Puṣya), Aśvi (Aśvinī), and Abhijit—this group is light; Mṛgaśiras, Citrā, Antya (Revatī), and Maitra (Anurādhā)—this quartet is mild.

Jyeṣṭhā, Ārdrā, Uragamālā (Āśleṣā), and Mūla—this group of seven names is declared to be "sharp" (*tīkṣṇa*). This [set] begins with the mobile and unstable (*cara-calādi*). As for the Moon (*śaśī*), the Sun (*ina*), Mars (*āra*), Mercury (*budha*), Jupiter (*guru*), Venus (*śukra*), and Saturn (*śani*): this is what is meant—they are respectively the mobile (*cara*), the stable (*sthira*), the earth-born (*bhuvaḥ*), the friendly (*mitra*), the light (*laghu*), the soft (*mṛdu*), and the sharp (*tīkṣṇa*). Such are the names of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). Thus it has been said: "The Sun is stable and the Moon is mobile;
[these are] the lamps of the auspicious moments (*muhūrta*)."

"O Lord of Sages, Mars is said to be fierce, Mercury is mixed, Jupiter is light, Venus is mild, and Saturn is sharp. (5) Consideration of the conjunctions of portents and so forth: One should avoid the three stars beginning with Ārdrā from the water-born [Mṛgaśiras] (i.e., Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣya); from the Vasus (Dhaniṣṭhā), the two beginning with Pauṣṇa (Revatī and Aśvinī); from Jīva (Jyeṣṭhā), the two beginning with Āryamaṇ (Phalgunī and Maghā); from the Sun (Hasta), the two beginning with Tvāṣṭra (Citrā and Svāti); from Vaiśvānar (Kṛttikā), the eight beginning with Mūla (Mūla, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, Pūrvabhādrapadā, Uttarabhādrapadā); from Jyeṣṭhā, the two beginning with Ambu (Pūrvaphalgunī and Uttaraphalgunī). Regarding the planets: eight [muhūrtas] for the Sun, five for Mercury, and all twenty-eight for the others, according to the day of the week and the lunar day. (6)

"From the Sun onwards, one should sequentially abandon these asterisms during the seven days for auspicious undertakings"—this is the remainder [of the verse]. Therein, on Sunday, one should abandon three asterisms starting from Dvīśa (Dhaniṣṭhā): Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣak, and Pūrvābhādrapadā. On Monday, starting from Udakoḍuta (Pūrvāṣāḍhā), one should abandon three asterisms: Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Abhijit. On Tuesday, starting from Vasubhata (Dhaniṣṭhā), one should abandon three asterisms: Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣak, and Pūrvābhādrapadā.

On Wednesday, one should avoid the three asterisms beginning with Pauṣṇa (Revatī), namely Aśvinī and Bharaṇī. On Thursday, one should avoid the three asterisms beginning with Kṛttikā, namely Rohiṇī and Mṛgaśiras. On Friday, one should avoid the three asterisms beginning with Jyeṣṭhā, namely Uttarāphālgunī, Hastā, and Citrā. On Saturday, one should avoid the three asterisms beginning with Ārdrā, namely Uttarāphālgunī, Puṣyā, Āśleṣā, Maghā, and Citrā. By this, the yogas of Utpāta (calamity), Mṛtyu (death), and Kāṇa (blindness) are described. Likewise, from the Sun, one should avoid two asterisms each.

One should avoid [the following]: on Sunday, the asterisms Yamamagha (Pūrvaphalgunī) and Bharaṇī; on Monday, Svāṣṭra (Citrā) and Dvidaiva (Viśākhā); on Tuesday, Vaiśvātṛ (Uttarāṣāḍhā); on Wednesday, Vasu (Dhaniṣṭhā) and Mūla; on Thursday, Amalaśata (Kṛttikā) and Śatatārakā (Śatabhiṣaj); on Friday, Jyeṣṭhā and Kabhra (Rohiṇī); and on Saturday, the two Budhas (Pūrvāṣāḍhā), namely Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā. These should be abandoned.

In this section on what is to be avoided (*tyājyaprakaraṇa*), that which is to be avoided on each day has been stated. Regarding Saturday, some claim that *Revatī*, *Hasta*, and one's birth star (*janmabha*) constitute the *Yamaghaṇṭā* yoga; however, this is baseless. Since the ancient teacher Trivikrama has already mentioned the *Mṛtyu* yoga in relation to *Hasta*, it is written according to Trivikrama’s view: "On Saturday, in the month of Āṣāḍha, [the asterisms] Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Śatabhiṣaj, as well as the two Āṣāḍhās. Thus, the two Āṣāḍhās are prohibited.

Now, when the sun is on Sunday and the lunar day (tithi) is the first, or when it is the seventh lunar day, in the conjunction of these two, eight [inauspicious yogas] arise. Similarly, when Mercury is on Thursday and the lunar day is the first, in the conjunction of these two, five [yogas] are to be avoided; thus it is for all combinations of lunar days and weekdays.

One should abandon all thirteen [tithis] as follows: the twelfth on Sunday, the eleventh on Monday, the tenth on Tuesday, the ninth on Wednesday, the eighth on Thursday, the seventh on Friday, and the sixth on Saturday; thus say Saṃvartaka and Krakaca. These are the *utpāta*, *mṛtyu*, *kāṇa*, *janma-bhaya*, *maitra*, *saṃvartana*, and *krakaca* yogas. (6) Now, the *pravṛtti-horās* and *kulikas* of the days.

Half a *rājya* (one and a half *ghaṭikās*) is for Yuyutsum; one and a quarter (*sapāda*) for Anuyuk; from there, the commencement of the *vāra* (weekday) is a *horā* of two and a half *ghaṭikās* for the Lord of the Day (the Sun). For each subsequent planet, that [duration] is the same. The *yāmārddha* (half-watch) for the Moon is four, seven, two, five, eight, three, six, and one [units]; Kulika is known to be at the end of the day. At night, it is one less than the sum of the [preceding] units.

One should take half of the night from among the nights and add it to the measure of the day. Then, one should add fourteen *ghaṭikās* together with fifteen palas plus one-quarter (*sapādāḥ*). When joined with those, the commencement of the weekday (*vāra*) occurs. If the remainder of the night is less than sixty [palas], it is counted from the start of the night; if it exceeds sixty, it is counted from sunrise. Thus ends the *Muhūrtadīpaka*. From the commencement of the weekday, the *horā* arises.

What are its characteristics? It consists of two and a half *ghaṭīs*. That which possesses two and a half *ghaṭīs* is the *horā* of the lords of the day and the weekdays (*vārāhāṇām*). For example: the first belongs to the lord of the day; the second to the sixth from him; and from that, again, to the sixth. In this manner, there would be twenty-four *horās* in a day and night (*ahorātre*). And so says Śrīpati: "In the commencement of the weekday, the *kālākhya-horās* (time-named *horās*) are the two *nāḍīs* [of the day] divided by five."

"The lords of the days and so forth are the Sun, Venus, Mercury; the Moon, Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars in sequence. Thus, starting from the lord of the day, among those [planets], the *horās* of the Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus are excellent; the *horās* of the Sun, Mars, and Saturn are ordinary, and are therefore middling. As for the statement of Śrīpati: "Whatever rite is prescribed for a particular planet on its own day, all of that is likewise performed during its *kālahorā*."

Now, from the Sun (Ravi), one should abandon the following [muhūrtas] as forbidden: on Sunday, the fourth, seventh, second, eighth, fifth, fourth, and sixth; on Monday, the seventh; on Tuesday, the second; on Wednesday, the fifth; on Thursday, the eighth; on Friday, the third; and on Saturday, the sixth. This is the forbidden *vāravelā*. Furthermore, from the Sun, the *muhūrta* known as *tithyaṃśa* is also forbidden.

A fifteenth part of the day and night is a *muhūrta*. That which is the *kulika* is as follows: on a weekday, it is known to be the *kulika* when it is equal [to the number of the weekday] in direct order from the first, or equal in reverse order from the fourteenth, being an even number. On Sunday, it is the fourteenth *muhūrta*; on Monday, the twelfth; on Tuesday, the tenth; on Wednesday, the eighth; on Thursday, the sixth; on Friday, the fourth; and on Saturday, the second.

On a Sunday night, the *kulika* occurs at the first muhūrta; on a Saturday night, at the thirteenth; on a Friday night, at the eleventh; on a Thursday night, at the ninth; on a Wednesday night, at the seventh; on a Tuesday night, at the fifth; on a Monday night, at the third; and on a Sunday night, at the first. These *kulikas* are prohibited for auspicious undertakings. As it has been said: "The *kulikas* occur at the muhūrtas numbered by the Manu (14), Sun (12), Earth (1), Tithi (15), Veda (4), Pakṣa (2), and Rona (6)."

"During the day they are solitary, but at night they are censured in auspicious rites. Thus it was said by Śrīpati: "Whatever rite is prescribed on the day (vāra) of a particular planet, all of that is likewise ordained for its *kālahorā*. This is stated by Śrīpati regarding necessary duties. Now, concerning *viṣṭi*: On the bright fortnight, in the second half of the lunar days beginning with the eighth and the new moon (*rākā*), *viṣṭi* occurs first; on the dark fortnight, in the first half of the lunar days beginning with the seventh and the fourteenth (*bhūta*).

That face [of the Viṣṭi-cakra] is auspicious at the beginning of the first watch (yāma) of the day during the bright fortnight, on the fourth and eleventh lunar days; thereafter, it occupies the western petal. On the eighth and fourteenth days, the Viṣṭi is likewise in the eastern petal of the bright fortnight. In the dark fortnight, on the third and tenth days, the Viṣṭi is in the western petal; thereafter, on the seventh and fifteenth days, it is in the dark [petal]. (16) [Regarding the verse beginning with] "In Svāti": *Note: The term "Laghu-dhruva" refers to the three fixed asterisms: Rohiṇī, Uttara-phalgunī, and Uttara-bhādrapadā. "Kaṇṭha" refers to Jyeṣṭhā. "Riktā" tithis are the 4th, 9th, and 14th lunar days. "Vadhvā" means "of the bride. "Śukre" refers to the planet Venus. "Dvirāgama" means a second marriage.*

Among these yogas, the entry into the house of a newly married bride is auspicious in Svāti, Mūla, and the *laghu* and *dhruva* nakṣatras—where *mūla*, the *laghus* (Hasta, Jyeṣṭhā, Anurādhā, and Abhijit), and the *dhruvas* (Rohiṇī and the three Uttarās) are combined; as well as in the *mṛdu* nakṣatras, Maghā, and Karṇa—where the *mṛdus* (Mṛgaśiras, Citrā, Svātī, and Anurādhā), Maghā, and Karṇa (Śravaṇa) are combined—and likewise in Vāsava (Dhaniṣṭhā).

Regarding that, he states what is to be avoided: having excluded (projhya) the *riktā* and *bhadrikā* lunar days as well as the *bhadrā* lunar day, and likewise the days of the Sun, Mercury, and Mars; in an odd year—namely the third or fifth—one should avoid the eastern and southern directions; this is declared to be the rule for the "double-return" (*dvirāgama*). On the lunar day prescribed for the journey, one should avoid the *riktā* and *vajita* days, and on the odd-numbered lunar days, one should avoid the asterisms such as Svāti and Mūla as previously stated.

In this regard, according to local custom, they perform a second arrival [of the bride] during the Festival of Lights (Dīpotsava); concerning this, he recites: "Neither the fault of Venus (Śukra), nor the fault of Jupiter (Jīva), nor the strength of the stars, nor the strength of the moon need be considered; for the first arrival of a new bride, they declare the Festival of Lights to be auspicious. (16) Now follows the consideration of the auspicious and inauspicious regarding the first menses, as well as the moment for the ceremonial bath.

The months of Bhādrapada, Madhu (Caitra), Jyeṣṭha, Pauṣa, and Śuci (Jyeṣṭha); the festival days; the eighth, twelfth, and Riktā (fourth, ninth, and fourteenth) lunar days; the sixth day; the days of the waning moon; the asterisms of Aśleṣā, Ārdrā, Mūla, Maghā, Kṛttikā, and the inauspicious days—these are not auspicious for the first pregnancy. Having abandoned the twilight hours, the Riktā days, the eighth, the Tīkṣṇa (Agni) asterism, Aśvinī, the last (Revatī), Maghā, Kṛttikā, and the inauspicious days, one should perform the *āplava* (purificatory bath) for her. 17. Regarding the verse beginning with "The months":

These factors do not bring auspicious results for a newly married woman at her first *ārtava*, that is, the first appearance of menstruation. Which ones? The months of Bhādrapada, Madhu (Caitra), Ūrja (Kārttika), Pauṣa, and Śuci (Āṣāḍha)—these five months are not desired. As for the lunar days (*parvan*), they refer to the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) and so forth; the eighth, the twelfth, and the "empty" (*riktā*) days—meaning those accompanied by the sixth (*ṣaṣṭhī*)—are likewise unfavorable. Furthermore, the "evil days"—Sunday, Tuesday, and Saturday—are not desired.

Upakṣama, Pitṛ-pūrṣikāntaka, Miśra, Dvīśānala, Indrabha, Jyeṣṭhā, Sarpa (Āśleṣā), and Ārdrā—these are the supreme [inauspicious] items regarding the twilight periods (*saṃdhyā*). In the first menstrual period (*prathamarajas*), these do not bestow auspiciousness. If she should conceive during these very times, then the pacification (*śānti*) mentioned by Kauśika and written down here must be performed. Immediately after that, she should perform the ritual bath (*ṛtusnāna*). Regarding purity therein, it is said: the Riktā lunar days, the eighth day, the Tīkṣṇa [nakṣatras], Jyeṣṭhā, and Ūraga-mūla [are to be avoided].

Having avoided the Aśvinī, Aśvinī, Revatī, Mṛgaśirā, Kṛttikā, and the day of Ku (Wednesday), as well as Sundays, Tuesdays, and Saturdays—this is the auspicious *āplava* (bath) for her who has reached puberty, as well as the purification bath (*malasnāna*) after menstruation. 17. Now, the auspicious time for conception (*garbhādhāna-muhūrta*): Having joyfully avoided the Mūla, Maghā, and Antya (Śatabhiṣaj) constellations, the first night of a Śrāddha, the new moon (*kuhū*), the half of the lunar fortnight, the fourteenth day, and the first four nights; on the sixth, eighth, and tenth days from the onset of menstruation, when the Moon is auspicious, one’s own wife is a most excellent [partner] for conception.

"Kheṭaḥ kaṇṭakakoṇagaiḥ... [Verse 18]. Regarding the phrase "having abandoned": during the menstrual period (*ārtava*), at the time of *ṛtu*, one should joyfully approach (*gacchet*) one's own wife, that is, one's beloved. Where? During the even nights (*samatīṣu*), namely on the sixth, eighth, tenth, twelfth, and fourteenth days. Having done what first? [The preceding verse provides the answer.]

Excluding the four nights following the period of menstruation; excluding the constellations Mūla, Maghā, and Revatī; excluding the preceding night of a *naimittika-śrāddha* as well as that day and night; excluding the new moon (*kuhū*) and the conjunction of the moon with the sun (*amā*); and further excluding the half-month [of the dark fortnight], the eighth, and the fourteenth—provided the moon is present and its strength is auspicious.

When the benefic planets—Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus—are situated in the *kāṇḍakas* (the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses), in the *koṇas* (the 5th and 9th houses), or in the 3rd, 6th, and 11th houses; and when the Sun, Mars, and Saturn are situated in the 3rd, 6th, and 11th houses; furthermore, in the *nṛyogas* (male yogas) mentioned in the *Jātaka* texts—such as the *Ojaḥpuruṣa-yoga*—one should declare a male birth. In the *pāṃśaka* divisions, if the Moon, Sun, Jupiter, and Moon are endowed with strength and occupy even signs, one should predict a female birth; if they occupy odd signs, a male birth.

The essential meaning is that, according to such yogas as "the Moon and Venus [are favorable] for a man in an odd [sign], and Mars in an even [sign]," and so forth, on any weekday—Mars, Jupiter, or the Sun—and under any one of the asterisms Mṛgaśīrṣa, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Mūla, Hasta, or Śravaṇā, when Jupiter is in an odd *lagna* (ascendant) and situated in a trine (*trikoṇa*), a woman who has reached her fertile period (*ṛtumatī*) should approach [her husband]. 18. [This concludes] the Muhūrta for the *Puṃsavana* and *Sīmanta* ceremonies.

The *sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair) rite should be performed in the sixth or eighth month, under the asterisms of Mūla, Jyeṣṭhā, Diti (Pūrvaphalgunī), Viṣṇu (Śravaṇa), Sūrya (Hasta), or Śaśin (Mṛgaśiras). The *puṃsavana* (rite for ensuring a male child) should be performed in the third or fifth month when the Moon is in its own or its lord’s sign, or when it is aspected by Jupiter; it should be done on a Tuesday, Thursday, or Sunday, with a masculine ascendant, while malefic planets occupy the sixth, third, or eleventh houses, and benefics occupy the fifth, ninth, fourth, or tenth houses, avoiding the twelfth and eighth. (Verse 19) Regarding the phrase "under Mūla": among these conjunctions, the *sīmantonnayana* sacrament is performed. Under which ones? In the sixth or eighth month, or according to family custom.

The asterisms Mūla, Ījya (Jyeṣṭhā), Puṣpa (Puṣya), Āditya (Punarvasu), Viṣṇu (Śravaṇa), Sūrya (Hasta), Śaśī (Mṛgaśiras), and Śaśin (Mṛgaśiras)—during these lunar mansions, in a month measured as the third or fifth [lunar day], the *puṃsavana* and *rakṣābandhana* rites should be performed, provided that its lord—the lord of that month, or the lords of the third, fifth, sixth, and eighth months—is capable and exceedingly powerful.

The lords of the months as declared in the *Jātaka* are as follows: "For the stages of the embryo (kalala), wealth (dhana), sprout (aṅkura), bone (asthi), skin (carmaja), and consciousness (cetana), Venus, Mars, Jupiter, the Sun, the Moon, Saturn, and Mercury are the lords. Thereafter, the lords of the [remaining] months are said to be, in order, the lords of the Ascendant, the Moon, and the Sun. The auspicious or inauspicious results are similar to those of the lord of the month. When one of these [lords] is strong, and the Moon is aspected by it or by a benefic, on the day of any one of Mars, Jupiter, or the Sun, in a masculine portion of the ascendant (puṃbhāga-lagna) at an odd degree, or in an odd sign, while malefic planets [are situated]...

When auspicious and excellent planets occupy the sixth, third, and eleventh houses, and when the fifth and ninth houses are in quadrants (the fourth and eighth), it is a *muhūrta* for the *dīpaka* rite. When auspicious planets go to the twelfth (*ripha*) or eighth (*ariṣṭa/mṛtyubha*), they are said to be "going to the twelfth or eighth"; however, the *puṃsavana* and *sīmantonnayana* rites do not occur when [malefic] planets are in the twelfth or eighth. [This also applies to] the *gaṇḍāntas*, the birth-time, the naming ceremony, and the *muhūrta* for the first feeding.

In the case of marriage and birth, Gaṇḍa and Antaka are inauspicious during the following periods: the last two *nāḍīs* of Aśvinī, the first two *nāḍīs* of Bharaṇī, the last two *nāḍīs* of Maghā, and the first two *nāḍīs* of Mūla; likewise, the first two *nāḍīs* of Anurādhā and the last two *nāḍīs* of Svāti. Furthermore, Plava is not desired when the Sun, Jupiter, or Mars are in the Lagna, nor when Mercury, Jupiter, or Venus are in a quadrant (*kendram*), provided they are in *mṛdu*, *dhruva*, *cara*, or *kṣipra* signs. (Verse 20) Regarding the verse beginning with "Aśvinī": Gaṇḍa and Antaka are inauspicious during the times of marriage and birth.

As for how much that [time] is, he says: at the end and beginning of Aśvinī and Revatī—that is, two *ghaṭīs* before Aśvinī and two *ghaṭīs* after Revatī—there is thus a period of four *ghaṭīs* known as *gaṇḍānta*. Likewise, two *ghaṭīs* before Maghā and two *ghaṭīs* at the end of Uraga (Āśleṣā) constitute the *gaṇḍānta*.

The final two *ghaṭīs* of Mūla and the first two *ghaṭīs* of Indrā (Jyeṣṭhā) constitute a *gaṇḍānta*. Thus, the *gaṇḍānta* consists of four *ghaṭīs*. In another treatise, three types of *gaṇḍāntas* are mentioned: "The *gaṇḍānta* is said to be of three kinds, arising from the asterism (*nakṣatra*), the lunar day (*tithi*), and the zodiacal sign (*rāśi*)."

"Measured at nine, five, four, three, two, and one ghaṭikās. Now, regarding the impurity (plava) of childbirth and the ritual bath: it [is auspicious] in the asterisms of Maitra (Anurādhā), Antya (Revatī), Anila (Svātī), and the Dhruvas (Rohiṇī and the three Uttarās), as well as Indu (Mṛgaśiras); and on the days of Ravi (Sunday), Ījya (Friday), and Arai (Tuesday).

When Jupiter, Venus, Mercury, or Guru (Jupiter) is situated in a quadrant (kendraka), and when the Moon is in the Mṛdu, Dhruva, Cara, or Kṣipra nakṣatras—namely Mṛgaśīrṣa, Citrā, Anurādhā, Rohiṇī, the three Uttarās, Svātī, Punarvasu, Śravaṇa, Revatī, Śatabhiṣaj, Hasta, Puṣya, Aśvinī, and Abhijit—the naming ceremony (*nāmakarma*) is beneficial and grants one's desires. **The Muhūrta for Ascending the Cradle:** On a day free from Mars and Saturn, during the asterisms of Revatī, Aśvinī, the two Bharaṇīs, the Dhruva, and Cara nakṣatras, and when the Moon is in the eighth, eighteenth, sixteenth, twelfth, or tenth lunar day (*tithi*), the act of placing the child upon the cradle (*prekhādhiroha*) is auspicious.

In that wheel (*taccakra*), there are twenty-seven stars (*tārā*) situated in the four directions and in the center; from the Sun, they grant auspiciousness, death, work, weeping, and desired results according to their positions in the directions. (Verse 21) Regarding the *Pauṣṇa* [yoga]: In this conjunction, ascending a swing (*prekhā*) is auspicious during the two asterisms of *Pauṣṇa* (Revatī), the two *Ādhika* (Aśleṣā and Maghā), and the *Dhruva* (Uttarās) and *Cara* (Pūrvās) asterisms, on a day excluding Tuesday and Saturday, on the 32nd, 18th, 16th, 12th, or 10th day. In that wheel, within the circle of those stars, there are five stars in each direction from the Sun, and seven in the center.

Five auspicious stars (*tārās*) in the region of the head [of the zodiac] grant fortune; five in the south bring death; five in the west accomplish one's tasks; and five in the north cause weeping. These results apply to the stars situated in the four directions; those situated in the middle [of the zodiac] grant desired objects. The Muhūrta for the first exit (*niṣkramaṇa*) and the tonsure ceremony (*caula*): The exit [from the house] should take place in the fourth month, during the two months of Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada, under the asterisms of Punarvasu, Puṣya, Anurādhā, Svāti, or Hasta; it should occur at the rising of a movable (*cara*) sign and within its favorable portion (*lava*), avoiding Tuesday and the *Kṛttikā* nakṣatra.

Under the Citrā, Revatī, or Mṛgaśīrṣa nakṣatras, during the period of light motion (the northern course of the sun), and avoiding the Riktā tithis, Tuesday, Saturday, and Sunday, as well as the sixth lunar day, the new moon, the full moon, the junction days (parvan), and one's birth day, the tonsure ceremony is auspicious. Regarding "without desire": for a child who has been placed upon a swing, the first outing outside occurs in the third month; in the fourth month, the child's first outing and the viewing of the sun are auspicious.

In the two *Haribha* (Hasta), the two *Śravaṇas*, *Aditi* (Punarvasu), *Ijya* (Puṣya), the two *Indubhas* (Mṛgaśīrṣa), *Maitra* (Anurādhā), *Aśvinī*, and *Kara* (Hasta)—in these asterisms, during the rising of a movable sign (*cara-lagna*) or at its end, this is the *Meṣa-muhūrta-dīpaka*. Alternatively, one should perform the *niṣkramaṇa* (the first outing) when any one of the signs Cancer, Libra, or Capricorn is the ascendant (*lagna*) or its ninth-part (*navāṃśa*). What are the characteristics of that [ninth-part]? It should be free from Mars and Saturn, and avoided on Tuesdays, Saturdays, and the inauspicious lunar days (*raktātithi*). This is the meaning.

The rites of tonsure (*muṇḍana*) and the first hair-cutting (*caula*) are auspicious when performed under the asterisms of Citrā, Revatī, Mṛgaśīrṣa, and Jyeṣṭhā, during the period of light motion (*laghucara*), and avoiding the sixth lunar day (*ṛktā tithiḥ*), Tuesday (*āro bhaumaḥ*), Sunday (*sūryaḥ*), and Saturday (*arkajo mandaḥ*). Furthermore, one should perform the *caula-karma* while avoiding the sixth lunar day, the first day of the fortnight (*pakṣati*), the first day of the month (*pratipad*), the new moon (*parva*), the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), the day of birth, the natal asterism (*janmanakṣatra*), and the natal day. Now, regarding the ritual of shaving (*kṣaurakarma*): The *caula* is auspicious under the asterisms of Citrā, Aśvinī, Revatī, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Puṣya, Hasta, and Jyeṣṭhā, during periods of light motion, and on the days of Mercury, Moon, Venus, and Jupiter.

One should perform auspicious acts such as shaving, avoiding the *riktā* lunar days, the end of the fortnight (*pakṣānta*), festival days (*parvan*), the night, and the two twilights (*saṃdhyā*). (1) If a man undergoes a haircut on the fifth, fourth, eighth, sixth, third, or ninth day of the lunar month under the asterisms of Anurādhā, Uttarā-phalgunī, Uttarā-āṣāḍhā, Uttarā-bhādrapadā, Kṛttikā, or Maghā, he becomes equal to the four-faced Brahmā; endowed with great strength, he does not die for many autumns. (2) The Sun causes a month to pass [in its transit]; likewise, the Son of the Sun (Saturn) bestows seven months of good fortune, while Jupiter (Bodhana) grants five months.

The sages beginning with Prādurga have declared that for the purpose of shaving, seven [days] are auspicious for Mars, ten for Jupiter, and eleven for Venus. (3) In the case of the movable signs, the asterisms are Svāti, Citrā, Aśvinī, Revatī, Mṛgaśiras, Puṣya, Hasta, Jyeṣṭhā, Svātī, Punarvasu, Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Śatabhiṣaj; and on the days of the Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus, the rite of shaving should be performed.

Having avoided Maitra (Anurādhā), Anurādhā, Vidhibha (Śatabhiṣaj), Rohiṇī, Vahibha (Kṛttikā), and Pitṛbha (Maghā)—these being unfavorable—and having set aside the end of the fortnight, the first day (pratipad), the junctions (parvan) such as the new moon and full moon, and furthermore, leaving the *riktā* tithis and avoiding the Sun, Mars, and Saturn, one should have the hair-shaving ceremony performed. 22 The Muhūrta for the First Feeding of Solid Food (*annaprāśana*): In the asterisms of Puṣya, Citrā, the light ones (Aśvinī, Revatī, Punarvasu, Hasta, Svātī, Anurādhā, Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj), the Cāndra (Mṛgaśiras), the Dvidaiva (Viśākhā), Jña (Mercury), Guru (Jupiter), and Śukra (Venus); having avoided the New Moon, the eighth lunar day, Sundays, and the *Nandā* tithis among the days of the week. [End of commentary].

Excluding the twenty-seventh and eightieth [asterisms], and avoiding the fourth, ninth, twelfth, eighth, and sixth asterisms from the Moon when it is not in a benefic sign, the consumption of food by women during these periods results in death. Regarding the term *pauṣṇa*: [the asterism] Revatī.

Regarding these conjunctions (*yoga*), the first feeding of children (*annaprāśana*) should be performed under the following asterisms: Poṣṇa (Revatī), Pauṣṇa (Revatī), Tvaṣṭra (Citrā), the light ones (Anurādhā, Hasta, Svātī), Dhruva (the fixed stars: Rohiṇī, Uttarā-phalgunī, Uttarā-bhadrapadā, Uttarā-aṣāḍhā), Aditi (Punarvasu), the pair of Hari (Śravaṇa and Śraviṣṭhā), Aindava (Mṛgaśiras), and Abhijit. Among these, it should be done on Wednesday (*budhavāra*), Thursday (*gurau* or *jīva*), or Friday (*śukre*). It must not be on the new moon (*darśa* or *amāvāsyā*), the eighth lunar day (*aṣṭamī*), Sunday (*haridina*), or the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*). Nor should it be during the *nada* [conjunction].

Excluding the new moon, the sixth, and the eleventh lunar days, as well as the day of birth, the time of birth, the ascendant (*lagna*), the asterism (*ṛkṣa*), and the zodiac sign (*rāśi*)—having completely avoided these and the eighth house from them—and when the benefic planets occupy the angles (*kendras*), the ninth, the eighth, or the twelfth houses (leaving the first, fourth, seventh, tenth, fifth, and eighth houses), and when the Moon is free from the sixth and eighth houses, for a man it occurs in the sixth month, and for women and girls in the fifth month.

The first feeding with solid food (*annaprāśana*) is auspicious. (23) The Muhūrta for ear-piercing (*karṇavedha*) and wearing ornaments (*bhūṣaṇadhāraṇa*): In the *Maitra* (Anurādhā), *Mṛga* (Mṛgaśiras), and the final two asterisms (*Śravaṇa* and *Dhaniṣṭhā*), when each is separately conjoined with benefic planets, and when the head (*mūrdhan*) or the feet (*pāda*) are occupied by Jupiter, provided there are no malefic planets; furthermore, in an odd year, avoiding the months of Caitra, Pauṣa, and the month of birth, and the day of birth; and having avoided the asterisms of Śravaṇa for piercing, the asterisms of Aśvinī, Puṣya, Dhaniṣṭhā, and the five *kara*-asterisms (Hasta, Citrā, Svātī, Viśākhā, Jyeṣṭhā) for wearing ornaments—this is auspicious. (24) Regarding "in *Maitra*": in this conjunction, *śravovedha*—the piercing of the ears—is auspicious.

O Maitreya, the piercing of the ears (karṇavedha) is auspicious when the Moon is in Mṛgaśīrṣa, Anurādhā, or Puṣya; when the last lunar mansion (Revatī) and Śravaṇa are each associated with two stars; when there are two ears (the two ears being pierced); when there are two hands (the two hands being held); when benefic planets occupy the third and eleventh houses (vyaya); when the Ascendant (lagna) is joined by Jupiter; when it is devoid of malefic planets; when the Ascendant is occupied by a benefic; during the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa); in an odd-numbered year; and having avoided the month of Madhu (Caitra), Pauṣa, the day of birth, and the month of birth—these are the conditions for an auspicious ear-piercing according to the *Muhūrtadīpikā*.

Now, regarding the wearing of ornaments upon the piercing of the ears, he says: In the tenth [nakṣatra], Aśvinī, Puṣya, Revatī, Vasubha (Vāsava), Dhaniṣṭhā, and in the five stars beginning with Hasta—namely, Hasta, Citrā, Svātī, Viśākhā, and Anurādhā—one should wear ornaments for the pierced ears, such as bracelets and the like, which are well-known in the world, including the *cūḍā* (ear-ornament) and so forth. In this regard, the astrological diagram (*cakra*) is applied. 24.

The asterisms from the Sun’s nakṣatra are three, five, three, two, seven, two, one, three, one, and one; these are the presiding deities of the Sun, Mars, Venus, Rāhu, Mercury, Jupiter, Saturn, Ketu, and the Moon. Among these, the benefic ones are auspicious for the bracelets on the hands, while the malefic ones are for the ear-ornaments. [Verse 25] Regarding the phrase "three, etc.": For the bracelets (pāṇivalaya), which are ornaments like conch-shells, starting from the Sun's asterism (sūryarkṣa), there are three, five, three, two, seven, two, one, three, one, and one asterisms; these are the deities of the Sun, Mars, Venus, Rāhu, Mercury, Jupiter, Saturn, Ketu, and the Moon respectively.

First, the Sun has three [asterisms]; Mars has five; Venus has three; Rahu has two eyes; Mercury, the knower, has seven mountains; Saturn has two eyes; Jupiter has one; and the Moon, the glāu, has three; Ketu has the earth, which is one—these are the *dhiṣṇyas* (asterisms) that exist. Among them, the gentle ones are those belonging to the Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus.

Furthermore, on the three Karṇa asterisms (Śravaṇa), on the three Śravaṇas, in Aśvinī, in Anila (Svātī), in Pitrya (Maghā), in Bhāgya (Pūrvā-phālgunī), in Mṛga, in Īśabha (Ārdrā), in Dvidayita (Viśākhā), and during the Saumya days—the weekdays of Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus—and on the day of the Sun (Ravi)—the tortoise-shells and their circular bands should be worn. || 25 || [End of commentary] 29. The Muhūrta for the Mauñjī ceremony (girdle-threading).

In the three asterisms beginning with Hasta, on the second and twelfth lunar days; in the conjunctions of the Sun and Saturn, and separately in the Moon; when Venus and Jupiter are strong; when Mars is in the sixth, eighth, or first house; when Venus avoids the eighth and seventh houses; during the bright fortnight; on the two second days, the fifth, the three tenth days, during auspicious *lagnas*, and during the five months of the hot season—on these occasions, the investiture of the sacred thread (*mauñjī*) is performed. (26) [The commentary begins: "Hastādīti" (Regarding the phrase "beginning with Hasta").

Among these yogas, the binding of the *mekhalā* (sacred thread) with a *mauñjī* cord is best for Brāhmaṇas. It should be performed on any of the three lunar days beginning with the third (*ka-hasta*), on the last day of the fortnight (*antya-hari*), on the two days beginning with the first (*aditi-dvandva*), separately on Punarvasu and Puṣya, on Revatī and Aśvinī, on Śravaṇa and Dhaniṣṭhā, and on the lunar mansion of the Moon (*candra-bha*) which is Mṛgaśīrṣa. It should be done when there is strength in Venus and Jupiter, and when there is favorable planetary transit (*gocara-bala*) for Jupiter, Venus, and the Moon. Furthermore, it should be performed during the five months beginning with Māgha, specifically in the bright fortnight (*dhavala-pakṣa*), on the two days of the second lunar day (*dvitīyā-dvaya*), and on the fifth, tenth, and third days (*pañcamyāṃ daśamī-traye*).

On the tenth, eleventh, or twelfth lunar day, during an auspicious *lava* or a gentle *lava*, having avoided the sixth and first houses, and having avoided malefic planets from the ascendant—namely Venus, Mars, Saturn, and Rāhu—and having avoided the Moon; having avoided the twelfth and sixth houses, and having avoided the planet Venus; and having avoided all planets from the eighth house, leaving the ascendant and reaching the twelfth or sixth house [for the Moon], the rite of the sacred thread (*mauñjī-yajñopavīta*) should be performed. (26) [This concludes] the Muhūrta for the commencement of learning (*vidyārambha*).

In the asterisms of Mūla, Aśvinī, and the five of Mṛga (Mṛgaśīrṣa, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Āśleṣā, and Maghā), in the three [asterisms] beginning with Śara (Pūrvaphalgunī, Uttaraphalgunī, and Hastā), and on days ruled by Venus, Jupiter, and the Sun—provided they are free from the *anadhyāya* periods and devoid of malefic planets—in the fifth year of a child, the undertaking of learning (*vidyodyama*) is exceedingly auspicious. However, in the asterisms of Rohiṇī, Kṛttikā, and the three Uttaras (Uttarāphalgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Uttarābhādrapadā), the science of archery may be pursued, but no other branch of knowledge should be undertaken. Regarding the word "Mūla": in these aforementioned yogas, the undertaking of learning—that is, the commencement of studies—for a child is auspicious. In which ones? In Mūla, Aśvinī, and the five of Mṛga; and in Karā (Hastā). This concludes the *Muhūrtadīpaka*.

In the asterisms of Śasta (Pūrvaphalgunī), Abhaya (Pūrvabhādrapadā), Hastā, Citrā, Svātī, Karṇa (Śravaṇā), and the three asterisms beginning with Tripūrvā (Pūrvāphalgunī, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and Pūrvabhādrapadā); on the days of Mercury, Venus, Jupiter, and the Sun; and on the weekdays of Wednesday, Friday, Thursday, and Sunday—in these [asterisms and days] during the fifth year, which is distinct [from others], one should avoid those non-study days (*anadhyāya*) that are joined with the first lunar day (*tithi*), as well as the *riktā* days. Furthermore, the eighth, ninth, thirteenth, fourteenth, new moon, full moon, the first day of the lunar fortnight, and the fourth day are prohibited. Also, the "group of four" starting from the thirteenth, and the three days beginning from the seventh, are forbidden.

The fourth [tithi] should likewise be avoided; these eight are the "throat-seizers" (galagrahas). Furthermore, the science of archery is not excellent when performed under the asterisms of Mṛgaśiras, Kṛttikā, and the three Uttaras, nor under Ārdrā. The Muhūrta for wearing clothes: Wearing garments is auspicious for men on the asterisms of Revatī, Aśvinī, the five Karas, Dhaniṣṭhā, and the three beginning with Budha (Mercury), provided they are joined with Puṣya, Punarvasu, or a Sthira (fixed) asterism and occur on a favorable lunar day.

On that wheel, gods, asuras, and humans are ninefold; in the corners and the center, there are ten nooses. The results are auspicious, desired, and beautiful, beginning with the numbers one, two, and so on. (28) Regarding "Pauṣṇa": in these conjunctions, wearing clothes (*cela*) is auspicious.

The wearing of clothes by men is auspicious under the asterisms of Revatī (Pauṣṇa), Aśvinī, and the five beginning with Hasta (Hasta, Citrā, Svātī, Viśākhā, and Anurādhā); furthermore, it is favorable under the asterism Dhaniṣṭhā (Vasubha) and during the three days of Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus; on lunar dates excluding the Riktās; and under the asterisms Puṣya, Punarvasu, the fixed (Sthira) ones, and the triad of Rohiṇī and the Uttaras.

On that wheel of the *sadvastra* (six-cloth), when divided into nine parts by nine divisions, gods (*sura*) dwell in the corners (*koṇa*), namely the four quadrants; demons (*asura*) dwell in the three middle squares; and humans (*nara*) dwell in the two squares at the end of the ten-fold enclosure (*daśāpāśa*). Among these, there are marks such as mud (*paṅka*), collyrium (*añjana*), and numbers (*aṅka*); because of the initial placement of mud and collyrium, there arise signs such as numbers and so forth. This concludes the commentary.

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), it should be understood that when [the cloth] is burnt or torn, the result is auspicious or inauspicious; it is auspicious in the portion belonging to the gods (*devāṃśa*), inauspicious in the portion belonging to the *rākṣasas* (*rakṣośa*), and the result is auspicious in the portion belonging to humans (*manuṣyāṃśa*). In this context, because of the association with clothing for women, one may also wear ornaments and the like. Thus it has been said: "In the group beginning with Karādi, Aśvinī, Revatī, and Dhaniṣṭhā are remembered [as auspicious]."

"And there is the wearing of pearls, gold, coral, and red garments. From the *Sajjanavallabha*: "In the asterisms of Aśvinī, Revatī, and the Vasus (Pūrvaphalgunī), and in the five fingers (the Hasta group), on the days of the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Venus, and on the days of the Moon, Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday, the wearing of pearls, gold, gems, coral, conch, ivory, and red garments leads to success. (1.28) Now, the Muhūrta for the Installation of the Sacred Fire (*Agnyādhāna*): "For the installation of the fire, the asterisms of Dhaniṣṭhā, Kṛttikā, Jyeṣṭhā, Āśleṣā, Mṛgaśiras, and the fixed (*dhruva*) and exalted (*utya*) signs (including Puṣya and Uttaras), as well as the lords of the Lagna (the rising sign), are auspicious when devoid of water-symbols (such as Śatabhiṣaj)."

If the Moon, Mars, Jupiter, and the Sun occupy the angles (kendras) and the triple-misfortune houses (upacayas), while the remaining planets are situated in the upacayas and not in the eighth house, there will be auspiciousness from the wife. (29) Regarding the term "udvāha": at the time of marriage (udvāha), during the performance of the wedding ceremony, and also at the time of the partitioning of wealth (vasu) when the division of property is being made, the establishment of the sacred fire (agnyādhāna) should be performed.

The asterisms Ārdrā, Indrāgni (Pūrvaphalgunī), Viśākhā, Śāna (Śatabhiṣaj), Jyeṣṭhā, Āgnimaya (Kṛttikā), Kṛttikā, and Mṛgaśiras are movable (cara). The fixed (dhruva) asterisms are Rohiṇī and the three Uttaras. Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius are fiery signs. Jupiter is the preceptor. Puṣya is the asterism. At the time of the lagna, it should be free from water [signs], meaning other than Pisces, Cancer, and Capricorn; and the Moon should be in a non-aquatic zodiac sign. The angles (koṇa) are the trines (5th and 9th houses); the quadrants (catuṣṭaya) are the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses, which are designated as the four angular points (kaṇṭaka-kendra-catuṣṭaya).

The seventh house, the ascendant, the fourth house, and the tenth house are the houses of *upacaya* (increase). The sixth, the eleventh, and the third houses are the remaining [non-*upacaya*] houses. When the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and the Moon are situated in these *upacaya* houses, and the remaining planets—Mercury, Venus, and Saturn—are all situated in *upacaya* houses excluding the eighth house, the installation of the sacred fire (*agnyādhāna*) will lead to the attainment of auspiciousness. 29. *Muhūrtadīpaka*. Now, the Muhūrta for royal consecration (*rājyābhiṣeka*).

In the month of Jyeṣṭha, under the asterism of Śravaṇa (Haribha), during a Mṛdu, Dhruva, or Laghu yoga, when the Moon is strong, and when the lords of the ascendant, birth, and year are situated in fixed signs or in head-rising (sīrṣodaya) ascendants; having avoided the Riktā tithis and the birth asterism, and with malefics in the third, sixth, and eleventh houses from the birth asterism, while benefics occupy the Upacaya houses in the ascendant—excluding the twelfth, sixth, and eighth—a royal consecration (abhiṣeka) is auspicious. ||30||

Regarding the phrase "in Jyeṣṭhā": during these yogas, the coronation of a king [is auspicious]. [The asterisms are: Jyeṣṭhā, Haribha (Śravaṇā), Śravaṇā, the Mṛdu-nakṣatras (Anurādhā, Citrā, Revatī, Maitra = Anurādhā), the Dhruva-nakṣatras (Rohiṇī, the three Uttarās), the Laghu-nakṣatras (Hasta, Puṣya, Aśvinī, Abhijit). Among these, the lord of the current period (tātkālikadaśā), Mars (Kṣmāja), the Sun (Arka), the lord of the ascendant at birth (Udayajanmapa), and the lord of the natal sign (Janmarāśīśa)—if all these are powerful (ojasvin), strong (balavattara), and situated in auspicious houses.

When the planets are situated in their own signs, exaltations, friendly signs, or trines, or in their own navāṃśas, and are endowed with splendor; when the ascendant is fixed (sthiratanu), such as Taurus, Leo, or Aquarius, or any other head-rising sign (śīrṣodaya); or when it is Gemini, Virgo, Leo, Aquarius, Aries, or Libra.

"Head-risings (śīrṣodayas) are prescribed. In any one of these ascendants, when it is conjoined with or aspected by a benefic planet—here, according to the reading "sahite" (conjoined), meaning on Mondays, Wednesdays, Thursdays, or Fridays; although the *Ratnamālā* also mentions Saturdays, thereby making Tuesdays and Sundays prohibited, while the other days are auspicious—one should perform [the rite]. Excluding the *riktā* lunar days, [the yoga] occurs in an ascendant that is a *tripaṣṭhāya* (the third, sixth, or eleventh house) from the natal planets or from the natal ascendant or natal sign. It is formed by malefic planets [occupying] the ascendant, and by benefic planets [occupying] the remaining houses, excluding the sixth and eighth.

The essential meaning is that the coronation of a king is auspicious when [the Moon] is free from the second, sixth, and eighth [houses]. || 30 || Now, the Muhūrta for bearing weapons: In the two Ādityas (Punarvasu and Puṣya), the Dhruva-nakṣatras (Uttarās), the Antyama (Revatī), the two Dvidaivate (Viśākhā and Anurādhā), the two Tvaṣṭṛs (Citrā and Śatabhiṣaj), Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), Maitra (Anurādhā), Aśvinī, and on the days of Saturn, Jupiter, and Venus; and when the Moon is aspected by benefics—then spears, swords, daggers, bows, arrows, armor, and *kaṇṭārikā* weapons should be borne by kings who desire victory, provided the Moon possesses strength. || 31 || [Regarding the verse beginning with] "dvayāditye": [The commentary follows].

In these yogas, weapons—that is, armaments—should be borne by kings who desire victory. Under which conditions? When the moon is aspected by benefics, when the moon possesses strength, and when it is in the asterisms of Punarvasu (the two Ādityas), the fixed asterisms (Uttaraphalgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Uttarabhādrapadā), the last one (Revatī), the two-dayited (Viśākhā), the two Tvaṣṭṛs (Citrā and Svātī), the two Varuṇas (Śatabhiṣaj and Śravaṇa), and Maitra-Aśvinī (Anurādhā and Aśvinī); and on the days of Saturn, Jupiter, and Venus.

The spear, the wrestler, the sword, the dagger, the javelin, the bow, the arrow, the shaft, the body armor, and the breastplate—these are the weapons to be carried. || 31 || Now begins the section on military expeditions (yātrā). One should set out immediately under the asterisms of Hasta, Mṛgaśiras, Śravaṇa, Āśleṣā, Puṣya, Dhaniṣṭhā, Āditya (Punarvasu), Anurādhā, and Revatī; the lunar mansions measured by three, five, seven, and eight [stars] are auspicious, as are the two Śaka years. One should avoid Saturn and the Moon, the six asterisms beginning with Śravaṇa, Jupiter, Jupiter’s asterism (Puṣya), the asterism of the Lord of Gods (Jyeṣṭhā), the asterism of the Pitṛs (Maghā), the first three asterisms (Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā), Venus and the Sun, Mercury, Mars, and the two asterisms of Aryaman (Phalgunī), as well as the letters 'A', 'Kā', and the Riktā days. || 32 ||

Regarding the term "haste" (the Hasta nakṣatra): among these yogas, the journey or departure is auspicious during the following asterisms: Hasta, Indu (Mṛgaśiras), Śravaṇa, Āśleṣā, Puṣya, Vasu (Dhaniṣṭhā), Āditya (Punarvasu), Maitra (Anurādhā), and Antyabha (Revatī). One should avoid the three stars beginning with Kubera (Ardra) and Ervatam (Abhijit). Furthermore, from the east (the eastern direction), one should avoid two asterisms—Jyeṣṭhā and Mūla. On Saturdays and Mondays, one should avoid the eastern direction. One should avoid the six asterisms beginning with Śravaṇa on Thursdays in the southern direction.

One should avoid the asterisms Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Puṣya, Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Śukra (Śravaṇā), and Ākai (Āśleṣā) when traveling toward the west. A wise person should also abandon the two asterisms Aryaman (Pūrvā-phalgunī) and Uttara-phalgunī, as well as Hasta, when traveling toward the north. Furthermore, one should avoid the solar days (tithis) that are occupied by the Sun, Mars, or Saturn, as well as the *rikta* days. As it has been said: "For one who travels, one should avoid the fourth, ninth, and fourteenth lunar days, as well as the *viṣṭi* karana."

Furthermore, there appear golden horses, elephants, and excellent chariots, as well as wealth, cattle, and elephants. Moreover, regarding the asterisms, one desiring victory in battle should avoid the first half of the asterisms of Aśvinī, Yama (Bharaṇī), and Ahi (Āśleṣā) when setting out. According to the opinion of Uśanas, the second half of Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, Svātī, and Viśākhā are entirely auspicious for travel. On a Wednesday, this journey is auspicious. (32) Now, the auspicious omens:

A swan, a cow, a fruit, a flower, a milky gem, a prostitute, curd, a horse, an umbrella, a mirror, honey, a blazing fire, wine, meat, weapons, a maiden, a deer, a mongoose, a blue jay, a peacock, a jar filled [with grain], a woman accompanied by her son, a sweet-spoken person, musical instruments, a fly-whisk, a scholar, a cloth-dyer—these, when seen on a journey, are auspicious. (33) Now he speaks of omens: "Brahmins," etc. These objects, when seen on a journey, are auspicious.

Who are these: Brahmins (*vipra*), twice-born men (*dvija*) numbering one or more; cows; fruit, flowers, milk; gems starting from crystal (*sphaṭika*) up to diamonds (*vajra*); a courtesan (*veśyā*), an ordinary woman (*sāmānyavanitā*); curds (*dadhi*); an elephant (*ibha*), a large elephant (*gaja*); a horse (*aśva*); a parasol (*chatra*), a sunshade (*ātapatra*); a mirror (*ādarśa*), a looking-glass (*darpaṇa*); honey (*madhu*), beeswax (*kṣaudra*); a blazing-tufted fire (*jvalacchikhī*), a non-flying fire (*alamāna*); liquor (*surā*), wine (*madya*); meat (*māṃsa*), raw flesh (*apakvāmiṣa*); a weapon (*astra*) such as a sword (*khaga*), a javelin (*bhallaka*), or a shield (*kheṭaka*); a maiden (*kanyā*); a deer (*mṛga*), a black antelope (*eṇa*); a mongoose (*nakula*); a blue-jay (*cāṣa*), a blue-winged bird; a peacock (*mayūra*), a crested bird (*śikhaṇḍin*); full jars (*pūrṇaghaṭā*).

"A woman accompanied by her son, speech that is well-spoken, words employed with auspicious blessings, and the fourfold musical instruments: stringed instruments such as the lute (vīṇā) are declared as *tata*; percussion instruments such as the drum (*muraja*) as *sannaddha*; cymbals and the like are known as *ghana*; and wind instruments beginning with the flute (*vaṃśa*) as *suṣira*. This [woman]—[along with the commentary]—is one of the musical instruments among the thirty-six [auspicious items].

A yak-tail whisk, fanning with the wind, washed garments—such items as these found near a washerman; furthermore, pleasant speech, the sound of the Vedas, the sound of voices, and likewise the resonance of drums and other instruments are auspicious. The sight of a mongoose, a blue jay, or a peacock is also excellent. A goat, a bharadvāja bird, or a [cuckoo] bird seen is auspicious. (33) Now, the ill omens:

Wood, leather, grass, fire, cotton, salt, bones, charcoal, oil, molasses, a barren woman, an enemy, one with disheveled hair, Kṛṣṇa (Vāsudeva), one who has applied medicinal ointments, a eunuch, a libertine, buttermilk, mud, fat, a naked person, a matted-haired ascetic, a dark-skinned person, food, a shaven-headed person, sneezing, a traveler, one who is dejected, one who is intoxicated, one who is exhausted, a drop of fluid, and evil speech—these are not auspicious when seen during travel. (34) Regarding "wood" and so forth: these objects, when seen while traveling, are not auspicious.

What are these? Wood such as fuel; leather such as footwear; grass such as fodder; a snake; cotton such as that from the *karpāsa* plant; five kinds of salt—namely, black salt (*kālalavaṇa*), rock salt (*saindhava*), sochal salt (*sauvarcala*), sea salt (*sāmudraka*), and *yavakṣāra* (though these are included among medicinal substances, they are specifically mentioned here); medicinal herbs such as *sāji* and *śārāva*; bone and tooth; charcoal (which is wood whose fire has been extinguished); oil; a barren woman (a woman who has not given birth); and a man who is impotent.

Anointed with oil; medicinal powders, pills, and the like; a eunuch or impotent man; excrement or feces; buttermilk; mud or mire; animal fat; one whose garment is wet; one with matted hair; black gram, mung beans, sesame seeds, and so forth; a shaven-headed ascetic; a mendicant; a sneeze or hiccough; a renunciant; a wretched person; one who is very intoxicated; one who has vomited; one who is leaking [fluids]; one who is falling; and evil speech such as "Go away! or "Where will you go?"—these are inauspicious. (34)

Now, the auspicious moment for laying the foundation (rambhamuhūrta). In the months of Kārttika, Phālguna, Mārgaśīrṣa, Vaiśākha, Nabhas (Śrāvaṇa), Bhādrapada, Pauṣa, and Āṣāḍha; when the moon is in a sign presided over by Jupiter, Jupiter, or the Sun; and when the Moon is in Hasta, Śravaṇa, or Aśvinī; the commencement of the door should take place. The door facing east is auspicious in Aries, Taurus, Gemini, and Cancer; facing south in Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces; facing west in Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, and Virgo; and facing north in Cancer, Leo, and Leo. (35) Thus ends the section on the month.

The commencement of a house or a building site (*vāstuprārambha*) should be performed during these lunar months: Phālguna, Mārga, Mādhava, Nabhas, and Pauṣa. *Phālguna* is well known; *Mārga* refers to Mārgaśīrṣa; *Mādhava* is Vaiśākha; *Nabhas* is Śrāvaṇa; and *Pauṣa* is well known. It is stated in the *Vāstuśāstra*: "Building a house and so forth in Caitra causes grief; in Vaiśākha it bestows wealth; in Jyeṣṭha it brings death; in Āṣāḍha it takes away cattle; and likewise in Śrāvaṇa it destroys learning."

"In the months of Bhādrapada and Āśvina, there is strife; in Kārttika, the destruction of wealth; in Mārgaśīrṣa and Pauṣa, grain; in Māgha, fire; and in Phālguna, prosperity. The commencement of a house should be performed when the moon is in the asterisms of Śravaṇā, Rohiṇī, the three Uttarās (Uttaraphalgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Uttarabhādrapadā), Mṛgaśīrṣa, Citrā, Puṣya, Hasta, Svātī, the two Viśākhās (Viśākhā and Anurādhā), Dhaniṣṭhā, and Śatabhiṣaj; on the days of Saturn, Venus, Mercury, or Jupiter; and when the sun is in the signs of Taurus, Pisces, or Aries. However, for these [specific] kings, the house should have its entrance facing east when the sun is in Scorpio, Aries, or Libra.

In the pair of signs beginning with Aries (the twins), the female sign is Virgo; in Capricorn, the male sign is Sagittarius. For these, a house facing the southern door is auspicious. In Taurus, Libra, and Aquarius, a house facing the western door is auspicious. In Cancer, Aśvinī (Pisces), Sagittarius, and Leo, a house facing the northern door is auspicious. || 35 || From Leo, in this house, one should move clockwise through the corners starting from the direction of Yama (south). The remaining [signs] have their faces turned away and their tails pointing elsewhere; an empty space equal to the sky (zero) is auspicious.

In the house of Mīnādeva, the Ṛṣabha altar is to the right (apasavya); from the bow (cāpa) to the east, it is to the left (savya) in sequence; the door is in the direction of darkness (the west), not facing the good (the east). [36] From the lion (siṃha)... etc.

In this house, during the three transits (saṃkrāntis) of the Lion [sign], one should rotate the face, back, and tail of the serpent Śeṣa clockwise from the northeast (īśāna) corner; the other [direction] is empty, and digging in that empty direction is auspicious. During the transits of Leo, Virgo, and Libra, the face of Śeṣa is in the northeast, the back in the southeast (āgneyī), the tail in the southwest (nairṛtī), and the empty space in the northwest (vāyavī); there, the excavation should be made.

Thus, during the three transits beginning with Scorpio (Vṛścika), the head does not enter the southeast corner; the tail is in the corner [southwest], the tail-end in the northwest, and the burrow in the northeast. Likewise, during the three transits beginning with Aquarius (Kumbha), the head is in the southwest, the tail in the northwest, the tail-end in the northeast, and the burrow in the southeast. In this manner, one should calculate the three positions—Pisces, Aries, and Taurus—in a temple; for a reservoir of water, one should calculate them starting from Capricorn in the same way.

And so it is stated in the *Muhūrtacintāmaṇi*: "In the construction of a temple, a house, or a reservoir, one should visualize Śeṣānana (the face of Śeṣa) starting from the direction of Śambhu (North) in sequence; when the Sun is in Pisces, Cancer, or Leo, one should contemplate [the directions] from the mouth to the back in the three signs [of the zodiac]. Also, in the *Daivajñavallabha*: "When the Sun is in Aries, the head is in the East; when in Bhādrapada (Virgo), it is in the South; and when in Mārga (Capricorn), it is the serpent's face in the West."

"In the months of Tapa (Śrāvaṇa) and Tapasya (Māgha), [the entrance] should be in the west; in the triad of months beginning with Jyeṣṭha, it should be in the north"—this calculation of the directions starting from Kanyā (Virgo) that has been made follows the Vāstuśāstra. "The wise declare the entrance to be in the east during Bhādrapada, Āśvina, and Kārttika; in the three months from Mārgaśīrṣa to Phālguna, it is in the south; and in the bright fortnight of Phālguna, it is in the north. Regarding water, it is likewise in the north.

"When the field is divided into eight by eight, one should draw squares starting from the Sun (the southeast). Therein, one should not dig where Saturn and Mars are located, nor where the serpent (Rāhu) is situated," so it is stated by Rājavallabha. A pit dug in the east-facing [square] is for the Yama direction (south); a pit in the northeast is for the Īśāna direction (north); digging in the southeast is likewise for the western direction; and similarly in the north. The mouth [of the pit] is in the southwest corner, or the digging is for the Śaṅku [direction], according to the *Muhūrtadīpaka*.

By virtue of the statement "the establishment [of the altar]," the month of Bhādrapada follows after Śrāvaṇa-pūrṇimā; however, since the sun's entry into Leo (Siṃha-saṃkrānti) occurs at that time, Rāmadaivajña and others have calculated from Leo in the *Muhūrtacintāmaṇi*. Alternatively, the calculation is made from Taurus (Ṛṣabha), by counting counter-clockwise (apasavya) or by turning to the left. Regarding the altar—whether for a wedding, a pavilion, or the Vedic fire-installation (*śrautādhāna*)—digging is prescribed. Furthermore: "From Taurus on the altar, from Leo in the house, and from Pisces in the temple, a triad [of signs] is auspicious."

The serpent (Nāga) moves through the creation, [occupying] the altar (Vedī) and the abode of Rudra, excluding [the center]. In the northeast (Īśāna), fire (Agni), and northeast, these are Mercury (Bu), Jupiter (Gu), Venus (Śu), and the Sun (Śa). [The sequence is: Meṃ, Vu, 8, 3, 4, 9, 11, 7, ₹, F, 10, Ra, Gṛha, Vu, Gu, Śu, Śa, Ma, Bu. In the northwest (Vāyavya), Mercury (Ma), Venus (Vu), Jupiter (Gu), 2, 3, 4, Nita, Vāyavya, 11, 15, 16, 7, 12, 1, 2, 18, 10, Ke, Īśāna, Agni, 11, 23, Agni, 3, 4, 5, 12, 1, 19, 0, 19, 9, 7, Pūrva, 9, 10, 11, Dakṣiṇā, 16, 7, 8. The deities of the directions are: Water (Jala) in the north; Rāhu is eternally in the northwest, 9, 10, and the west.

In this year 1678, [the calculation yields] Vāyavya 789 and 415; many wander here in the excavation, performing the turning (valana). That which was spoken by Rājavallabha, situated within sixty-four squares, is accompanied by its commentary.

One should avoid the days of Mars and Saturn, as well as the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*), the *riktā* tithis, the *parvan* days, the full moon (*pūrṇimā*), the new moon (*amāvāsya*), and the eighth lunar day (*aṣṭamī*). Then, in that wheel—the *halacakra*—one should perform the calculation starting from the asterism (*nakṣatra*) traversed by the Sun; the results, whether auspicious or inauspicious, are to be known according to the asterisms [in the sequence]: three, three, five, three, three, five, three, three, three, three, five arrows [five], and three. In the constellations Anurādhā, Rohiṇī, the three Uttaras (Uttaraphalgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Uttarabhādrapadā), Maghā, Mūla, Aśvinī, and Ārdrā—which are the fixed (dhuva) nakṣatras—and in Puṣya, the sowing of seeds is indeed auspicious when the Sun has traversed the sign of Capricorn; however, it does not yield good results in the three [asterisms] beginning with Mṛgaśiras, nor in Āśleṣā. In the Tuṇḍa (the mouth of the wheel), the stars are auspicious; elsewhere, these four and five [asterisms] are for the time of sowing seeds in the field. Regarding the verse beginning with "maitra": in these yogas, the sowing of seeds is auspicious.

In which [asterisms] are there auspicious results? In Maitra (Anurādhā), Anurādhā, Revatī, Vasubha (Dhaniṣṭhā), the three Karas (Hasta, Citrā, Svātī), Maghā, Mūla, Aśvinī, Candra (Mṛgaśirā), Dhruva (Rohiṇī and the three Uttarās), and Puṣya; in the diagram of the serpent's body, starting from the asterism occupied by the Sun, three stars each in the head yield auspicious results, but not in the neck. In the belly (tunda), twelve asterisms beginning with Arka (Punarvasu) are auspicious. In the tail (puccha), four asterisms are auspicious, and elsewhere outside the tail, five asterisms are auspicious—these are the four in the tail and the five elsewhere.

At the time of sowing seeds and in the threshing floor, two evil fruits arise. (4) *Muhūrtadīpaka*: The auspicious moment for administering medicine and ploughing. Medicine is beneficial in the asterisms of Revatī, Aśvinī, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Mṛgaśiras, Hasta, Śravaṇa, Āśleṣā, Anurādhā, and the two corners (Pūrvā-phalgunī and Pūrvā-bhādrapadā), excluding the new moon, the full moon, the sixth lunar day, and the Sun’s birth asterism. (41) Regarding "Pauṣṇa": in these aforementioned yogas, medicine is effective.

In which of these [constellations] does medicine become effective? [The answer is: In Pauṣṇa (Revatī), Aśre (Aśleṣā), Aśvinī, Aditi (Punarvasu), Bhadvaya (Puṣya), Śaśima (Mṛgaśiras), Hastāttraya (Hasta, Citrā, Svātī), Karṇādhaya (Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj), Maitra (Anurādhā), and Koṇapabha (Mūla).
